stem: A client with a newly diagnosed, complex cancer asks why the case will be presented at a multidisciplinary tumor board. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?

options.A: Specialists from different disciplines review the case together and develop a coordinated treatment recommendation that can be discussed with the client by the treating team.
options.B: The tumor board replaces the client's treating clinicians and makes a final treatment decision that does not require further discussion with the client.
options.C: The meeting is primarily administrative and is used to schedule procedures rather than to review clinical information and treatment options.
options.D: Only one oncology specialty reviews the case so that differing perspectives do not complicate the treatment plan.

rationale: The National Cancer Institute defines tumor board review as a treatment-planning process in which cancer physicians and other healthcare specialists meet to review and discuss new or complex cancer cases and decide as a group on the best treatment plan. Participants may include medical and radiation oncologists, surgeons, pathologists, radiologists, genetics professionals, nurses, social workers, and other specialists. The tumor board supports coordinated multidisciplinary planning; it does not eliminate the treating team's responsibilities or the client's role in informed decision-making.
educational_objective: Explain the purpose of a multidisciplinary tumor board as coordinated clinical review by multiple cancer-care disciplines that informs, rather than replaces, patient-centered treatment planning.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — tumor board review; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — multidisciplinary; NCI-ASCO Teams in Cancer Care Delivery

source_claim_supported: NCI describes tumor board review as multidisciplinary treatment planning in which cancer physicians and other healthcare specialists review and discuss new or complex cases together; multidisciplinary cancer care includes expertise from multiple specialties and team-based care requires shared information and responsibilities.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the original definition-only tumor-board item into a client-teaching scenario using direct NCI definitions and current NCI team-care material. Replaced weak, obviously incorrect distractors with plausible role and decision-making errors. Added the critical distinction that tumor-board recommendations support coordinated planning but do not eliminate the treating team's responsibilities or the client's informed participation.
audit_findings: Original item tested rote recognition with distractors that were too obviously implausible for a professional nursing examination.
NCI directly defines tumor board review as multidisciplinary review of new or complex cancer cases for treatment planning.
The final item avoids implying that a tumor board can override informed consent or independently replace the treating clinicians.
Distractors now test confusion about patient autonomy, administrative versus clinical function, and multidisciplinary versus single-specialty review.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, or unresolved role conflict.
